listings.name: Cenotaph
listings.content: Built in 1923 in honour of the fallen soldiers of World War I and later also attributed to the ones from World War II. It is a copy of the more famous one in London. There is a ceremony on on the second Sunday of November to commemorate the fallen soldiers.

listings.name: City Hall
listings.content: Concert hall, theatre, and exhibition space. This cultural hub is famous for its dim sum restaurant.

listings.name: Government House
listings.content: Originally the official residence of the British Governors of Hong Kong under colonial rule, since the handover back to China in 1997, it has been the official residence of the Chief Executive of Hong Kong. Only open to the public on specific open days that are usually published on the web-site in advance, usually once in the spring to coincide with the blooming of the flowers in the garden, and once in the autumn.

listings.name: Man Mo Temple Compound
listings.content: Consists of Man Mo Temple, Lit Shing Kung Temple and Kung Sor assembly hall. Man Mo Temple was built in the 1840s and is Hong Kong Island's oldest temple. It is nestled amongst antique shops, with the air full of smoke from hundreds of burning incense coils. While you are there, pop into one of the many antique shops to see some of the best Chinese and South-East Asian antiques in the world, and the many very clever fakes for sale.

listings.name: Statue Square
listings.content: Public square built in the 19th century with a number of royal statues. Now the only statue is of banker Sir Thomas Jackson. It is a relaxing place with plantings and fountains. The square is surrounded by some impressive buildings, including the HSBC headquarters and the Legislative Council.

listings.name: Jamia Mosque
listings.content: Constructed in 1890, it is the oldest mosque in Hong Kong.

listings.name: Ohel Leah Synagogue
listings.content: Orthodox synagogue built by Baghdadi Jews in 1902. Most of Hong Kong's Jewish community lives in the surrounding neighbourhood.

listings.name: Dr Sun Yat-sen Museum
listings.content: Exhibits on the life of Sun Yat-sen.

listings.name: Flagstaff House Museum of Tea Ware
listings.content: Museum of teapots and cups, with exhibits ranging from modern to 3000 years old.

listings.name: Hong Kong Museum of Medical Sciences
listings.content: The neighbour of one of the earliest hospitals in Hong Kong, Tung Wah Hospital, this museum shows how the healthcare system evolved from traditional Chinese medicine to modern Western medicine, via the establishment of numerous hospitals and the first medical school (now the University of Hong Kong), of which Dr. Sun Yat-sen was a student.

listings.name: City Gallery
listings.content: A celebration of planning proposals and infrastructure projects. Interactive features and devices give visitors the latest information on planning and infrastructure developments in Hong Kong.

listings.name: Hong Kong Visual Arts Centre
listings.content: Offers visual arts studios for artists as well as exhibition halls.

listings.name: Madame Tussaud's
listings.content: The usual Tussaud's waxworks with characters that appeal to Chinese interests.

listings.name: University Museum and Art Gallery
listings.content: The oldest museum in Hong Kong dating back to 1953 has a large permanent collection of Chinese antiquities as well as modern paintings. It also host exhibitions of contemporary and ancient art.

listings.name: Hong Kong Maritime Museum
listings.content: In addition to original artifacts, cannons, scrolls, ship's models and paintings, the galleries of Hong Kong Maritime Museum have over 25 interactive screens using the latest technology to introduce visitors to the vast range of stories and topics at the heart of Hong Kong's – and the world's – maritime story. You can learn of Poon Lim, the world record holder for solo survival at sea. See how a junk is built. Trace the development of China's trade routes from the Han to the Qing Dynasty. Investigate China Trade paintings. Hunt pirates. Load a container ship.
listings.price: $30, half price for seniors and students

listings.name: Trick Eye Museum Hong Kong
listings.content: The only Korean 3D museum in Hong Kong. It presents a magnificent collection of 3D art pieces. It features paintings on plain surfaces that magically appear to be three dimensional through the use of optical illusion. You are most welcome to touch, climb and interact with the amazing exhibits. You can also enjoy the free observation deck view of the beautiful Harbour View.
listings.address: Level 3, The Peak Galleria, 118 Peak Road, The Peak

listings.name: Chater Garden
listings.content: Adjacent to the Legislative Council Building, this is the place where disgruntled Hongkongers come to protest. Named after businessman Sir Paul Chater.

listings.name: Hong Kong Park
listings.content: A great place to relax in Central. Head for L16 cafe and bar which is one of the few places where you can eat and drink outdoors away from the traffic.

listings.name: Hong Kong Zoological and Botanical Gardens
listings.content: A small, free zoo with reptiles, primates, a jaguar, and rare and endangered birds and plants.

listings.name: Lung Fu Shan Country Park
listings.content: Hong Kong newest and smallest Country Park. Its proximity to the Peak makes it highly accessible and one is rewarded by a pleasant hike away from the crowds nearby. A convenient place to make a BBQ with great views over Victoria Harbour. Budding military historians will enjoy exploring Pinewood battery and other remnants of the Second World War.

listings.name: Central-Mid-Levels Escalator
listings.content: At 800 m long, this is the longest outdoor covered escalator system in the world. The escalator runs downhill from 6AM to 10AM and uphill from 10:30AM to midnight every day. Part of it near the bottom goes along Cochrane Street, and it's hard to miss. It goes from busy areas at the bottom to upscale residential neighborhoods at the top. For tourists it's not all that useful for transportation, but it's an interesting curiosity that CNN declared one of the world's coolest commutes.

listings.name: Mount Davis
listings.content: Walk up Mount Davis to see the abandoned Second World War-era gunnery fortifications. Take the steps up from Victoria Rd just west of Kennedy Town; or follow Victoria Rd until you reach the roundabout (about a kilometre), and take the mountain road up. The climb will take a while, but there are many ruins to explore, and great views. There's also a youth hostel at the top if you are too tired to make it back in one go.

listings.name: Sheung Wan Civic Centre
listings.content: Theatre and concert venue.
listings.address: 5/F., Sheung Wan Municipal Services Building, 345 Queen's Road Central,

listings.name: Wellington St
listings.content: Nice street with dried foodstuffs, various restaurants, majong pieces. Also check out Art Jam at 123 Wellington St. They provide you with canvas, paints and materials. From $200 to $500 depending on when you go and canvas size.

listings.name: Yan Shang Kee
listings.content: Rent a qipao to wear for a day while exploring Hong Kong.

listings.name: Dumpling House
listings.content: Great Beijing-style dumplings, avoid going there during lunch hour, because it is packed.

listings.name: Good Luck Thai
listings.content: Seating is both indoors and outdoors, very popular on weekends, nice atmosphere.

listings.name: Law Fu Kee
listings.content: Popular little restaurant serving congee and noodles.

listings.name: Wai Kee Congee Shop
listings.content: A good place to sample some traditional Hong Kong style food.

listings.name: XTC Gelato
listings.content: A popular place to get your fix of ice cream or frozen yoghurt.

listings.name: Zhong Guo Song
listings.content: Good Chinese food, without MSG and less oil.
listings.address: Wo On Lane, Lan Kwai Fong

listings.name: L16 Cafe and Bar
listings.content: Serves Thai and Italian food, but come for the location - not the food. A rare place to drink and eat outside away from the noise of Central.
listings.address: Hong Kong Park, 19 Cotton Tree Drive

listings.name: Maxim's Palace
listings.content: One of Hong Kong's most popular dim sum spots, featuring harbour views if you're lucky enough to score a window table. The atmosphere and food are very much in the classical dim sum tradition, a large, noisy hall with waitresses pushing around carts laden with goodies; try the siu mai (燒賣), har gao (蝦餃) and mango pudding. Dim sum served 11AM-3PM daily, expect to queue on Sundays (when the restaurant opens at 9AM). Try to gather a few people so you can try many different kinds, and expect to pay $100-200 a head. Don't confuse this with Maxim's Restaurant on the 2nd floor.

listings.name: Pizza Express
listings.content: Has a nice view overlooking the Mid-Levels Escalator.

listings.name: Yung Kee Restaurant
listings.content: This is a popular place for Cantonese-style roast goose and century eggs. Come early and make reservations as they have been known to run out of geese!

listings.name: Baci
listings.content: Pizza.

listings.name: Beirut
listings.content: Lebanese cuisine is top of the sheet. Lamb or chicken kebab and sisha. Nice decor but the food is a far cry from the real deal (particularly in taste).

listings.name: Tokyo Joe
listings.content: Japanese food.

listings.name: Fung Shing Restaurant
listings.content: Very local eatery known for its dim sum, which is cheap and good at $10 and up per serving. Open daily from 7:30AM for the dim sum breakfast crowd, but no English menu.

listings.name: Al Dente
listings.content: Italian cuisine. Serving large, medium quality dishes not too different from what you would find in an Italian bistro. Their pastas and meat dishes are better than their pizzas. Often full.
listings.address: 16 Staunton St, Soho (中環蘇豪士丹頓街16號地下)

listings.name: Ayuthaiya
listings.content: Thai cuisine. Serving quite authentic food in a stylish, dark environment.
listings.address: 35 Hollywood Rd, Soho (中環荷李活道35號)

listings.name: Brunch Club
listings.content: Neighbourhood-style Western coffee shop (pre-Starbucks style) specialising in brunch and breakfast, although dinner is also served. Customers are provided with a wide range of newspapers and magazines in English and Chinese. Clientele is mainly expatriate.

listings.name: Double Happiness Cafe
listings.content: Shanghai cuisine. Nice and simple little restaurant serving authentic Shanghainese dishes. Prices reflects that this is in the centre of Soho and comparable food can be found much cheaper elsewhere.

listings.name: Jashan
listings.content: Indian cuisine. Serves great curries and perfect naan. The lunch buffet is good value.

listings.name: Oola
listings.content: Away from the crowds in Soho, but worth the extra walk. International menu in a comfortable environment. Serves as both a place to eat or drink. Drinks are expensive.
listings.address: G/F, Centre Stage, Bridges St, Soho

listings.name: La Pampa
listings.content: Argentinian.

listings.name: The Peak Lookout
listings.content: Serving a range of international cuisine such as naan bread, Hainan chicken, and steaks in a 19th-century heritage building. Also has a pleasant garden patio.

listings.name: Percy Bakery
listings.content: A high quality bakery. Take away and delivery service only.
listings.address: Shop b, g/f, 68 Catchick St, Kennedy Town

listings.name: 8½ Otto e Mezzo Bombana
listings.content: Only Italian restaurant outside Italy to be awarded three Michelin stars.

listings.name: Bistro Bouchon
listings.content: French bistro focusing on steaks.

listings.name: Chez Patrick
listings.content: An excellent, Parisian-style French restaurant. The proprietor, Patrick, has a delightful obsession with foie gras which extends to creative dishes such as foie gras ice cream served as a first course.

listings.name: Chilli Fagara
listings.content: Sichuan cuisine. Great spicy dishes including the favourites you will find in Sichuan Province. This restaurant's ambitions appear to go further than just making the food as the mainland original implying that some might be disappointed. Somewhat overpriced but still good.

listings.name: Luk Yu Tea House
listings.content: Famous for the excellent tea and traditional dim sum. It is a popular meeting place for businessmen. They provide an English menu on request.

listings.name: Yung Kee Restaurant
listings.content: Established in 1942, this restaurant has enjoyed unparalleled success and was once named in the "Top Fifteen Restaurants in the World" by Fortune Magazine. Previously a humble BBQ house serving its renowned roast goose, it has evolved into a world-famous Cantonese restaurant. Dim sum is also served at lunch-time. Be prepared for a noisy environment at peak times, this type of restaurant is not for those seeking a quiet meal and is best experienced in a large group.

listings.name: HAHAClub
listings.content: For cheaper booze, you can try here.

listings.name: Works
listings.content: A good place for tourists to start on the gay bar-scene. Popular with expats and tourists alike, it is easily accessible in Central. Friday and Saturday are the most popular nights but do not expect many drinkers to arrive much before 11PM.

listings.name: 65 Peel
listings.content: A bar with a very Hong Kong aesthetic serving cocktails and a range of locally brewed beer.

listings.name: de België
listings.content: A bar specialising in Belgian beers.

listings.name: Craft Brew & Co
listings.content: A corner bar with a selection of craft beer on tap.

listings.name: The Globe
listings.content: Excellent beer pub, also has good menu aimed at western taste buds. It is also one of the few places that has Typhoon T8 on tap, a locally produced cask ale.

listings.name: Staunton's Wine Bar & Cafe
listings.content: A western-style restaurant with a bar on the ground floor and table service upstairs.

listings.name: Propaganda
listings.content: Famous gay club. Tends to get going after Works has faded.

listings.name: Bishop Lei International House
listings.content: Operated by the Catholic Diocese.

listings.name: Cosco Hotel
listings.address: Yick Fung Garden, 20-21, Praya Rd, Kennedy Town

listings.name: Jockey Club Mt. Davis Youth Hostel
listings.content: Great hostel almost at the top of Mt Davis, with good views over the city and plenty of fresh air, well away from the city bustle. Self-catering kitchen, with limited supplies sold in the hostel. Friendly staff.
listings.address: Top of Mt Davis Path, Mt Davis, Kennedy Town

listings.name: Lan Kwai Fong Hotel @ Kau U Fong
listings.content: A boutique hotel uniquely designed with a distinctive touch of oriental style. Each room's furniture, fabrics and artifacts are meticulously chosen displaying striking individuality. Awarded as "Asia's Leading Boutique Hotel" by World Travel Awards 2009.

listings.name: Ovolo Hotel – 286 Queens Road Central
listings.content: Boutique hotel that opened in 2012. 60 Rooms. Queen or twin mattresses, AppleTV, loot bag, rainfall shower, electric curtains, free minibar, free breakfast, free Wi-Fi, happy hour.

listings.name: Hotel Jen
listings.content: Rooms with free internet and views of Victoria Harbour and nearby mountains. Business centre, fitness and outdoor swimming pool available. Chinese and Western restaurants as well as bar.
listings.price: Listed rates from $1,243, discounted from $600, breakfast $152 (included for more expensive rooms)

listings.name: Mingle Place On The Wing
listings.content: Full sized suite provides separate living/work and bedroom areas.

listings.name: Ramada Hong Kong
listings.price: Generally from $900, can be discounted to $600
listings.address: 308 Des Voeux Rd West, Sai Ying Pun

listings.name: ibis Hong Kong Central & Sheung Wan
listings.content: Hotel begins at 5th floor. Harbour view rooms available, good views of Kowloon. Breakfast buffet available. Midway between Sheung Wan and Sai Ying Pun MTR stations. Kennedy tram is also available. Macau Ferry Pier is a short walk away.
listings.address: 28 Des Voeux Road West, Sheung Wan

listings.name: Conrad Hotel Hong Kong
listings.content: One of three elegantly appointed 5-star hotels at the conveniently located Pacific Place complex. 513 rooms, swimming pool, and health club. Amongst the five restaurants is Nicholini's.

listings.name: Four Seasons Hotel Hong Kong
listings.content: One of the most prestigious in Hong Kong, opened in 2005, 399 rooms, wall-to-wall windows with view of Victoria Harbour or Victoria Peak, two outdoor infinity pools, a 22,000 spa, and a fitness centre. The only hotel in the world with two 3-star Michelin restaurants.

listings.name: Island Shangri-La
listings.content: One of three elegantly appointed 5-star hotels at the conveniently located Pacific Place complex. The hotel comprises 531 rooms and 34 suites decorated with Asian-accented European furnishings. Facilities include a health club and swimming pool.

listings.name: JW Marriott Hotel Hong Kong
listings.content: One of three elegantly appointed 5-star hotels at the Pacific Place complex. Features 577 rooms, a swimming pool, 24-hour fitness centre, and six restaurants.

listings.name: Landmark Mandarin Oriental
listings.content: Boutique hotel, opened in 2005, 113 rooms, 25,000 Oriental Spa.

listings.name: Mandarin Oriental
listings.content: The chain's original and prestigious flagship. 502 rooms, spa, indoor swimming pool, and fitness centre. Michelin 3-star chef Pierre Gagnaire has lent his name and inspiration to, Pierre, the hotel's French restaurant.

listings.name: The Mercer
listings.content: Opened in 2011, 55-room boutique hotel, outdoor swimming pool, 24-hour fitness centre with complementary minibar, coffee and tea.

listings.name: Ovolo Hotel - 2 Arbuthnot road
listings.content: Design boutique hotel with Apple TV, free 1Gbps Wi-Fi, free breakfast at cafe, full wash and dry services, free mini bar, free local calls, 24-hour gym and flexible checkout. Smoke free. Free access to 9000 citywide hotspots

listings.name: Central Plaza
listings.content: Can be seen from most of Wan Chai. Central Plaza was the tallest building in Asia from 1992 to 1996, and the tallest in Hong Kong until 2003. It is possible to tell the time by the changing lights on the top of this building. During business hours, you can take the lift from the ground floor to the sky lobby on the 46th floor to get a spectacular free view of the harbour and the island. Another option for a free is view is from the observation lift in the Hopewell Centre at 183 Queen's Road East. This is one of the very few round towers found in the city. This glass lift can be taken from the 17th floor and the amazing journey to the 62nd floor takes about 90 seconds. Once at the top you can eat at the revolving restaurant on top of the building, or head back down again.

listings.name: Noon Day Gun
listings.content: The historic gun is fired every day at noon and once a year at midnight on New Year's Eve. To access the Noon Day Gun, enter the underground tunnel between the World Trade Centre and the Excelsior Hotel and follow the signs. Finding this tunnel is difficult and you might need to ask staff for directions. The tradition of firing a gun into Victoria Harbour everyday at noon dates back to the 1860s. It is believed that this is the gun referred to in Noel Coward's song "Mad Dogs and Englishmen".

listings.name: Golden Bauhinia Square
listings.content: The site of the ceremony in 1997 in which the United Kingdom returned Hong Kong to China. A flag raising ceremony is held here ever morning at 8AM, when the Hong Kong Police will perform foot drills and raise both the Chinese national flag and the Hong Kong flag to the accompaniment of the Chinese national anthem. Visit at night time for a stunning view of the neon-lit skylines of Kowloon and Hong Kong.

listings.name: The Old Wan Chai Post Office
listings.content: Now an Environmental Resource Centre, this building was used for over 70 years as a post office. This attractive building is the only declared monument in Wan Chai.

listings.name: Hong Kong Central Library
listings.content: Opened in 2001, Hong Kong's main public library looks over the playgrounds of Victoria Park. It is an impressive 12-storey structure that holds a vast collection of Chinese and English resources. Visitors will find exhibitions, wifi access, newspapers and magazines. There is a souvenir shop and a branch of Delifrance where you can relax.

listings.name: Ammar Mosque and Osman Ramju Sadick Islamic Centre
listings.content: The third mosque built in Hong Kong.
listings.address: No. 40, Oi Kwan Road, Wan Chai
listings.image: HK WC 灣仔 Wan Chai 日善街 Yat Sin Street June 2020 SS2 04.jpg

listings.name: Chai Wan Mosque
listings.content: The fifth mosque built in Hong Kong.
listings.address: Cape Collison Road, Tai Tam Gap, Chai Wan

listings.name: Fireboat Alexander Grantham Exhibition Gallery
listings.content: Exhibits firefighting stuff.

listings.name: The Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre
listings.content: One of Hong Kong's most outstanding buildings. If you are refused admittance, you can take a walk along the promenade at the front of the building to find the place where the British returned Hong Kong to mainland China. Paved in concrete, the modest plaza where the Handover took place in 1997 is home to two monuments; one takes the form of a giant golden bauhinia and the other looks like a chimney stack. The bauhinia tree is sometimes known as the Hong Kong orchid and has been adopted as the emblem of the SAR which features on the Hong Kong flag that flutters above the square. For the many tourists from mainland China, this place holds a special significance, so you can expect a steady stream or tour buses.

listings.name: Hong Kong Film Archive
listings.address: 50 Lei King Road, Sai Wan Ho

listings.name: Law Uk Folk Museum
listings.content: 18th-century Hakka village house.

listings.name: The Museum of Coastal Defence
listings.content: Despite its dry title, this museum is worth a visit if you enjoy military history.
listings.address: 175 Tung Hei Road, Shau Kei Wan

listings.name: Hong Kong Police Museum
listings.content: There are five galleries: Orientation describing the history of the force, Triad Societies and Narcotics describing the history of Triad Societies and narcotic problems, Police Then & Now describing the transformation of Hong Kong Police Force over the years, Current Exhibition exhibiting changing themes, and Heroin Factory exhibiting a heroin production site.

listings.name: Victoria Park
listings.content: Take some time to walk through it or to watch people play football on three fields. There is also a jogging track through the park. Victoria Park can also be reached by MTR Exit B at Tin Hau station. During the summer months you can use the public open-air pool in Victoria Park. The pool costs $19 for adults ($9 kids) and payment can be made by coins or Octopus card.

listings.name: Quarry Bay Park
listings.content: A good place to walk that provides an alternative view of the eastern end of the harbour, instead of the familiar one of the west. It also serves as a connection between SOHO east (a reasonably attractive restaurant and pub area) and Cityplaza shopping centre.

listings.name: Southorn Playground
listings.content: Amidst the skyscrapers of Wan Chai, Southorn Playground offers a scarce area of public outdoor space for football, basketball and has seating for those who just want to relax and watch.

listings.name: Gloucester Road
listings.content: Pronounced in the British way as Gloss-ter Road, this street is famous for car showrooms where the rich will spend and the rest will take photographs of themselves in front of their dream car.

listings.name: Horse racing
listings.content: Horse racing has been taking place at Happy Valley racetrack since 1846. Happy Valley is particularly impressive during the evening meets with the surrounding skyscrapers lit up. Unless you know the right sort of people your best chance of getting into the races is by the public entrance. Entrance will cost you just a few dollars and you will have the advantage of being at ground level next to the race track. Alcohol, especially beer, is sold at cheap prices. Unless you like fast-food, plan to eat before or after gambling away your holiday savings.

listings.name: Hong Kong Racing Museum
listings.content: Artificats and some of the largest exhibits in the world next to the track of the Happy Valley Racecourse.
listings.address: 2/F, Happy Valley Stand, Happy Valley Racecourse, Wong Nai Chung Rd, Happy Valley

listings.name: Hong Kong Academy of Performing Arts
listings.content: A venue for dance, music and drama.
listings.address: The Hong Kong Academy for Performing Arts 1 Gloucester Road Wanchai

listings.name: Hong Kong Cricket Club
listings.content: Private club but one restaurant is open to the public. If you're a cricket player, you can apply to join as a sports member.

listings.name: Chiu Yuen
listings.content: Small and usually packed eatery serving up a wide range of simple fare, but the crowd-pullers are the beef brisket noodles (a scarcely believable $13) and the homemade giant fishball soup ($16). Other branches are in Aberdeen and Causeway Bay.

listings.name: Tsui Wah Restaurant
listings.content: Clean and multilingual, this is a moderately priced cha chaan teng where even a non-Chinese speaker can easily explore. Aside from the typical cha chaan teng foods such as French toast, curry, baked rice, fried noodles, and Hong Kong style milk-tea, also try their famous fishball noodle in soup. Expect to share a table at peak hours.

listings.name: Cafe Kenon
listings.content: Where affordable Italian food meets Chinese expectations.
listings.address: Shop 208, 2/F Tai Yau Plaza, 181 Johnston Rd, Wanchai

listings.name: Tai Hing Roast Restaurant
listings.content: A Cantonese BBQ eatery. Roast pork, roast piglet, BBQ pork, roast goose, soy sauce chicken are all hanging in the front display window, available to eat in or take out.
listings.address: G/F, Shop J, Po Ming Bldg, 49-57 Lee Garden Rd, Causeway Bay.

listings.name: Loving Hut
listings.content: Serving vegetarian and vegan fast food at affordable prices.
listings.address: Shops B&C, G/F, The Hennessy, 256 Hennessy Rd

listings.name: New Bangkok Restaurant
listings.content: Friendly staff serving excellent Thai food.

listings.name: Hokkaido Dairy Farm
listings.content: Ham, eggs, toast and Japanese milk. Very good for a light breakfast or lunch.
listings.address: Shop A-B, G/F, 211 Johnston Road, Wan Chai

listings.name: 3.6.9. Restaurant Shanghai
listings.content: Great old style dive usually packed with locals especially at lunch. Shanghai style Chinese food, excellent and inexpensive Xaio Long Bao. About as authentic as you'll find in this part of the island.

listings.name: Baby Blue Cafe and Bar
listings.content: Western food served to meet Hong Kong taste buds.
listings.address: 3/F, Chuang's Enterprises Building, 382 Lockhart Road, Causeway Bay

listings.name: The Quarterdeck Club
listings.content: Fenwick Pier, Wanchai. This is one of the few harbourside restaurants. Slightly spoiled by the land reclamation nearby

listings.name: The Flying Pan
listings.content: On the corner of Lockhart Road and Luard Road. Look above Mes Amis and you will find the best place for breakfast and it's open all-day, everyday. This is the place where you can have a full-English washed down with a glass of lager at any time you prefer. It has an extensive menu catering for all preferences and a "frequent fryer" club if you want to keep going back. Staff are friendly and speak good English.

listings.name: Kung Tak Lam
listings.content: A delightful vegetarian restaurant serving Shanghainese cuisine. Hotpot, dim sum and noodles dishes are made with MSG free ingredients.

listings.name: Chun Kee Restaurant
listings.content: Serves typical Chinese food from dumplings to Peking Duck.
listings.address: 117-119 Shau Kei Wan Road, Sai Wan Ho

listings.name: Red Pepper Restaurant
listings.content: Causeway Bay (MTR: Causeway Bay). Sichuan cuisine; spicy dishes.

listings.name: Pho Saigon
listings.content: Extremely good Vietnamese restaurant serving traditional dishes including Pho and Vietnamese coffee. Expect to pay around $120.

listings.name: Tai Ping Koon Restaurant
listings.content: (太平館餐廳), 6 Pak Sha Road, Causeway Bay. Founded in Guangzhou in 1860, the three locations (two in Kowloon) have now become institutions of Canto-Western cuisine. Don't be put off by the touristy menu available in three languages, as the restaurant is very popular with locals. Some specialties are the Swiss sauce chicken wings, roasted young pigeon, smoked promfret, dried fried rice noodles with beef, and baked souffle. Reservation for a seating in their 1960-style room is highly recommended.

listings.name: Café One
listings.content: Causeway Bay, Open 24 hours a day, seven days a week. Fun & friendly informal dining from an open kitchen and an exciting buffet featuring a wide selection of Asian and Western cuisines.

listings.name: Tony Roma's
listings.content: International food. This branch has the advantage of an outdoor terrace that enables you to eat and drink above the noise of the streets below.

listings.name: Under the Bridge Spicy Crab
listings.content: This has become a Hong Kong institution that is famous for its Typhoon Shelter style crab. People come for the food not the interior which is basic.
listings.address: Shop 1-2, G/F, 414 - 424 Jaffe Road, Causeway Bay

listings.name: West Villa Restaurant
listings.content: Its signature dim sum is the cha xiu bao (叉燒包) or roast pork buns that is served steamed, fried or as rolls. One of the items is named "Big Brother Chaxiu" after Hong Kong's film star Jacky Chan (Big Brother) who is fond of its cha xiu buns.

listings.name: Cosmo Hotel Wan Chai
listings.content: This hotel is spanned across 23 floors and consists of 142 rooms and suites. Free shuttle bus services are provided for 15 locations. They also offer free use of smart phone, 4G internet, Wi-Fi, local and IDD calls to 9 countries.

listings.name: Fook Lam Moon
listings.content: The main branch of an old school Cantonese restaurant group with locations in Kowloon, Shanghai and Japan. Famous for luxurious delicacies such as abalone, and swallow's nest. More affordable specialties include roast suckling pig, crispy chicken, and steamed lotus leaf rice.

listings.name: The Coffee Academics
listings.content: Great coffee a short walk from Times Square in Causeway bay. Coffee is roasted on premise and they have an outside sitting area.
listings.address: G/F, Bigfoot Centre, 38 Yiu Wa St

listings.name: The Cafe Corridor
listings.content: Small coffee shop directly opposite Time Square. Entrance is really small so look carefully. Good coffee for $26.

listings.name: Café "1974"
listings.content: A coffee shop operated by Po Leung Kuk that also functions as the ICAC's museum. The shop was named after the year of establishment of the Independent Commission Against Corruption, and coffee is known to be one of the drinks available to detainees during interrogation. Good coffee at around $22.
listings.address: G/F, ICAC Building, 303 Java Road, North Point

listings.name: The Pawn
listings.content: Wan Chai. A Western-style bar and cafe in an attractive building that was once a pawn shop. It is away from the naughty parts of Wan Chai in one of the few historic buildings remaining in Hong Kong. It will appeal to visitors seeking a good range of imported beers and wines.

listings.name: Joe Bananas
listings.content: This is one Hong Kong's most famous and popular bars, and can be highly recommended to younger travellers. Drinks are competitively priced, and staff are helpful and friendly.

listings.name: Devils Advocate
listings.content: Popular with the rugby crowd with English pub food.

listings.name: Kangaroo Pub
listings.content: Australian sports bar. Has a book exchange.

listings.name: Carnegie's
listings.content: Rock music themed bar. Live bands playing occasionally, sports on multiple screens and a big screen, dancing the night away on the bar top.

listings.name: The Canny Man
listings.content: Scottish style Whiskey Bar with a free pool table.

listings.name: Skitz Sports Bar
listings.content: 5/F. Sports bar with pool tables, darts and big screens.

listings.name: The Wanch
listings.content: A good bar for music lovers with live music playing every night. There is also a showcase of local bands held over several days around the 1st of July every year.

listings.name: The Chapel
listings.content: Serves curry.

listings.name: The Jockey
listings.content: A relaxed British style pub that serves food. When the weather suits this is a great place to sit outside and watch the world pass by.

listings.name: Inn Side Out
listings.content: Also 'East End Brewing Company'.

listings.name: Moon Garden Tea House
listings.content: A calming location in a busy part of town where you can choose from over 70 types of tea and, for a price, enjoy the Chinese ritual of tea served in tiny cups. Food is also served.

listings.name: Dickens Bar
listings.content: Popular British-style sports bar in the basement of the Excelsior hotel. A good range of drinks and serves very good English food, including a notable curry lunch buffet.

listings.name: Wang Fat Hostel
listings.content: This hostel would go out of business competing against any hostel in any European city, but compared to the prisons of Chunking and Mirador Mansions, it's halfway decent. Single rooms go for $250-300 and dorms run about $170. There is one dingy kitchen and a few refrigerators. The staff are brusque but helpful and honest, and there is free wireless and a single molasses-slow computer with free internet for hostel guests.
listings.address: 3rd floor, block A, 47 Paterson St., Causeway Bay

listings.name: Yesinn Hostel
listings.content: The youth & budget hostel in Hong Kong Island. Provide Mix/Female Dorms and private rooms for backpackers, young people, internship and budget business travellers who are looking for a warm, local, homely atmosphere and an affordable quality hostel.Private rooms go from HK$260 and dorms run from HK$99.
listings.address: Flat B, 5th floor, Front Block, 294 King's Rd., Causeway Bay, Hong

listings.name: Sun Kong Hostel
listings.content: Block C, sixth floor. A few minutes walk from Causeway Bay MTR Station (exit E). Rooms are small but clean with daily maid service. There is a communal refrigerator for roughly ever eight rooms. Toilets tend to block rather easy though. Double rooms run at about $300 with singles being anything from $130 with a shared toilet to between $200 and $400 with a private one.

listings.name: Ibis North Point
listings.content: This inexpensive Ibis offers really tiny rooms in a 31-floor high building. The view towards the harbour is rather nice.

listings.name: Walden Hotel
listings.content: Walden Hotel is a 3-star business and leisure hotel which offers 54 guest rooms. Well equipped bedrooms include a desk area, tea and coffee making facilities, LCD television with satellite TV channels, full amenities, mini bar and free In-room Internet service.

listings.name: Lanson Place Hotel
listings.content: Lanson Place Hotel is five to 10 minutes walk from the MTR system. It's 20 minutes away from Central by taxi, and 20 minutes from Kowloon by MTR. If you want to take a breather, Vistoria Park is five minutes walk. Some of their in-room amenities include an LCD flat screen TV, wireless broadband Internet connection, and a personal safe. As for guest service, they provide 24-hour reception, concierge service, business centre, fully equipped gymnasium, and food delivery service.

listings.name: Cosmo Hotel
listings.content: This hotel spans across 23 floors and consists of 142 colour-coded rooms and suites and offers green amenities, free Wi-Fi up to 200 mbps, provides a smart phone with 4G Internet access and free shuttle services for 15 destinations.

listings.name: Mingle Place By The Park
listings.content: In the heart of Wanchai next to parks, public facilities, shopping centres, historical sites and close to the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre. The hotel has a business centre.

listings.name: Novotel Hong Kong Century
listings.content: A fairly reasonable 4-star hotel in the heart of Wanchai.

listings.name: Holiday Inn Express
listings.content: Comfortable, clean and next to the shopping action in Times Square. Breakfast has Western and Chinese options, with the Western options decidedly underwhelming. Internet is fast.

listings.name: Dorsett Wanchai Hotel
listings.content: An environmentally friendly “green” hotel having 454 superior rooms, premier rooms, grand deluxe course view rooms and suites. The hotel offers free Wi-Fi up to 200 Mbps, walk-in massage shower with rain shower head and coffee and tea-making facilities.

listings.name: Somerset Victoria Park Hong Kong
listings.content: This property offers studio and one-bedroom apartments, equipped with complimentary Wi-Fi and a smartphone with 3G data.

listings.name: Metropark Hotel Wanchai, Hong Kong
listings.content: The 4-star hotel underwent a multi-billion major renovation, representing a new and refreshing image. In heart of the city, equipped with LCD TV and broadband service.

listings.name: Grand Hyatt Hong Kong
listings.content: Overlooks Victoria Harbour. Has a direct connection to the Hong Kong Conventions and Exhibition Centre. Host to the renowned Plateau Spa.

listings.name: Lanson Place Hotel
listings.content: Causeway Bay. A small boutique hotel in a modern building with an old world European facade. Situated in a "less-busy" corner of Causeway Bay.

listings.name: Jia Boutique Hotel
listings.content: Causeway Bay. A 54-room boutique hotel designed by Philippe Starck. Complimentary in-room broadband internet access, breakfast, wine during cocktail hour, afternoon cakes, and California Fitness gym access. Some rooms with cooking equipment.

listings.name: The Park Lane Hong Kong
listings.content: Causeway Bay. This 810-room 4-star hotel may not be brand new, but it is in the heart of Hong Kong's shopping and entertainment district. Great views of either Victoria Harbour or Victoria Park. From $1380.

listings.name: Tsim Sha Tsui Clock Tower
listings.content: Built out of red bricks and granite, the Clock Tower peaks at 44 metres, and is topped by a 7-metre lightning rod. The top of the tower can be reached by a wooden staircase located within.

listings.name: Avenue of Stars
listings.content: A promenade to honour celebrities of the Hong Kong film industry, modelled on the Hollywood Walk of Fame.

listings.name: A Symphony of Lights
listings.content: The narration is in English M-W-F, Mandarin Tu-Th-Sa and Cantonese Su. You can also download the app for your preferred narration.

listings.name: Dialogue in the Dark
listings.content: An exhibition in complete darkness. Experience five different Hong Kong themed environments using your non-visual senses on a 75-minute tour with the help of a visually impaired guide. Reservations are recommended, especially for a tour in English or Mandarin instead of Cantonese.
listings.price: Weekdays $160, $90 for students and seniors; weekends $180, $100 for students and seniors
listings.address: Shop 215, 2/F, The Household Centre, Nob Hill, 8 King Lai Path, Mei Foo

listings.name: Hong Kong Cultural Centre
listings.content: Opened in 1989 and in a prominent position on the waterfront, it is a contender for being the most famous ugly building in Hong Kong. However, if you are a lover of the arts, don't judge this building by its bland exterior; inside the architects have created a superb space that really does justice to the sights and sounds of each performance.

listings.name: Hong Kong Heritage Discovery Centre
listings.content: Housed in former British colonial barracks, which are architecturally interesting in their own right. The centre houses one permanent (Explore our Heritage) and a couple of temporary exhibitions about Hong Kong's and China's history. There are also lectures, workshops and similar events.
listings.address: Kowloon Park, Haiphong Rd, Tsim Sha Tsui

listings.name: Hong Kong Museum of Art
listings.content: A fascinating, strange and elusive place. The entrance lies up one floor, mimicking the “temple” approach to the high altar of culture and art. Once you arrive on the first floor, you are bathed in light from the wall of glass that gives you a panoramic view of Hong Kong Island. The objects on show are Chinese ceramics, terracotta, rhinoceros horn and Chinese paintings. There is also a temporary exhibition space devoted to items from their own collection with additional lent material. There is also space for contemporary art produced by Hong Kong artists, most of whom have moved away from the traditional Chinese art forms to fusion art with North American and British influence, reflecting Hong Kong's colonial past.

listings.name: Hong Kong Museum of History
listings.content: The permanent exhibition, the Hong Kong Story, covers the history of Hong Kong from millions of years ago until the reunification with China in 1997. Exhibits are about the nature, culture and history of Hong Kong. Also special exhibitions changing every few months. Forget the idea that all of Hong Kong museums are frumpy and boring. The Hong Kong Story is a real must go and do, ideal for those who want to make sense of Hong Kong's vibrant past in an engaging and interactive way. Allow 2-4 hours.
listings.address: 100 Chatham Rd South, Tsim Sha Tsui

listings.name: Hong Kong Palace Museum
listings.content: A museum displaying artefacts from the Forbidden City in Beijing.
listings.price: Adults $50, concessions $25, entry is free on Wednesdays provided you book online
listings.address: 8 Museum Drive, West Kowloon Cultural District (西九文化區博物館道8號)

listings.name: Hong Kong Science Museum
listings.content: Large museum with many interactive exhibits including an energy machine and an airplane. A museum which decided to make an architectural statement about its purpose, yet somehow got it horribly wrong. This museum is primarily aimed at children. The maths puzzles and optical illusions on the top floor are challenging. There is a giant Rube Goldberg machine spanning the entire museum that is run for a few minutes every two hours. (Sections are being renovated during 2016.)
listings.address: 2 Science Museum Rd, Tsim Sha Tsui East

listings.name: Hong Kong Space Museum
listings.content: Small museum, with a basic history of space flight in static exhibits, including a single exhibit on Chinese space flight. It also has interactive exhibits, allowing you to fly a hang glider, work a space motion system, and simulate walking on the moon. It has a planetarium attached that shows movies projected onto the roof. Plan ahead if you want to see an English session, as most are Cantonese. It is fun for kids aged around 10 to 15 years.
listings.price: $10 on most days. Free on Wednesdays

listings.name: Lei Cheng Uk Han Tomb Museum
listings.content: Tomb from the Eastern Han dynasty (AD 25 - 220) discovered in 1955. Exhibition hall displaying pottery and artifacts from the excavation of the tomb.

listings.name: M+
listings.content: Museum of contemporary visual culture (architecture, design, animation, and visual art) with a local and global focus.

listings.name: Kowloon Park
listings.content: the location of a former British barrack. There, you will find not only pleasant gardens, but aviaries, museums, and sporting facilities, including Hong Kong's best swimming pool complex, which offers both indoor and outdoor pools. A wide range of swimming, diving and children's play-pools will appeal to kids of all ages, and their frazzled parents who are seeking a safe place for youngsters to play away from the traffic.

listings.name: Kowloon Walled City Park
listings.content: The Kowloon Walled City began as an enclave that remained under Chinese sovereignty when the New Territories and the rest of Kowloon were ceded to the British. After the fall of the Qing Dynasty in 1912, its legal status became disputed, and there was no effective government within the walled city as a result. The massive influx of mainland Chinese refugees after the communist takeover led to haphazard construction of high-rise buildings, resulting in a horrendous convolution of maze-like alleys, darkness, cramped space, unsanitary conditions and fire hazards. There was no effective police presence inside the city, and it was a hotbed of triads, prostitution and unlicensed doctors and dentists. The Walled City was notorious for drugs, vice and many things shady and criminal. In 1994, after so many years of being beyond the reach of the law, the colonial government struck a deal with the Beijing authorities and razed the place to the ground. The park that replaced it is very tame in comparison to its distinctive history, but it does offer a few clues and remnants from its colourful past, including the former yamen dating back to the Qing Dynasty. As of 2026 there is an exhibition within the park that has some simulacral recreations of the walled city.
listings.address: Tung Tau Tsuen Road, Kowloon City
listings.image: Kowloon Walled City Park 九龍寨城 02.jpg

listings.name: Nan Lian Garden
listings.content: A Tang-dynasty-style garden, part of the Chi Lin Nunnery complex.

listings.name: Shek Kip Mei Estate
listings.content: Built in the 1950s, this is one of the few remaining places where you can grasp the living conditions of Hong Kong during the 50s and 60s. Despite the march of progress promulgated by the Urban Renewal Authority, there are still a few blocks of flats remaining from the 1950s, which are still occupied. Walk from Shek Kip Mei MTR Station.

listings.name: Shanghai Street
listings.content: runs north-south parallel to Nathan Road and offers an easy to navigate urban transect. Start at the north-side of Kowloon Park and wander up to Langham Place, a modern shopping and hotel complex which is next to Mong Kok MTR station. Along the way you will experience Kowloon in its raw authenticity. This is not your regular tourist trail, but crumbling tenements and small-scale industrial and commercial outfits blur to form an urban landscape that will make you wish that you had brought your camera along.

listings.name: Marine Police Headquarters
listings.content: Dating back to 1884, it is an attractive colonial building that has been renovated to become a major tourism attraction with shops and restaurants.

listings.name: Sik Sik Yuen Wong Tai Sin Temple
listings.content: Next to Wong Tai Sin MTR Station, this is the most popular Taoist temple in Hong Kong. This is where many people ask for divine guidance by a practice known as kau cim (求籤), a practice that has all but disappeared in mainland China. Entrance is free, though voluntary donations are welcome.

listings.name: Kowloon Mosque and Islamic Centre
listings.content: The largest mosque in Hong Kong.
listings.address: No. 105, Nathan Road, Tsim Sha Tsui
listings.image: Kowloon Masjid and Islamic Centre from East 2.jpg

listings.name: Kowloon Park Swimming Pool Complex
listings.content: Offers a wide range of services, including an indoors Olympic-sized pool, a slightly smaller training pool, a diving pool, and a leisure pool for younger swimmers. During the summer months, the indoor pools are air-conditioned, whilst in winter the water is heated. During the summer season, there are four outdoor leisure pools that are popular with teenagers, but all age-groups make good use of the pools. A limited number of sun loungers are available.

listings.name: Tin Kwong Road Recreation Ground
listings.content: With a capacity of 3500, this is the home stadium of the Hong Kong national cricket team, who play separately from China.
listings.address: Tin Kwong Rd, Ma Tau Wai

listings.name: Hong Kong Coliseum
listings.content: Multi-purpose indoor arena with 12,500 seats. A famous landmark shaped almost like an upside down pyramid. Used for sport events, concerts and other things.

listings.name: Temple Street
listings.content: South of Mong Kok is a great place to eat Chinese street food. You have not been to Honkers unless you have eaten in this street. Temple Street, famously featured in Chinese cinema, is one of the few pedestrianised streets in Kowloon where you can sit, relax and watch the world pass by. Seafood is a popular choice, but most restaurants will provide you with an extensive English/Chinese menu that caters for most tastes. Frog is a tasty option, or try the oyster omelettes.

listings.name: Chungking Mansions
listings.content: Houses many budget Indian, Nepali and African restaurants. Touts at the front entrance will lead you to the restaurants via the small rickety lifts. Be warned that the competition between the touts can become very open, sometimes aggressive, so you should be prepared to make your choice as quickly as possible to avoid being dragged away to a restaurant that you did not really plan on going to. Chungking Mansions is one of the most (in)famous buildings in Kowloon. To many local people it is the very best place for cheap, honest, Indian or Nepali food, whilst others will condemn it as a rat-infested hell-hole with a good chance of diarrhoea thrown in for free. This is also a good (albeit shady) place to change money, with rates slightly better than on-the-street establishments.

listings.name: CitySuper
listings.content: A local upscale supermarket chain with pan Asian, Western style food and has its own food court in Harbour City on Canton Road, Tsim Sha Tsui.
listings.address: 3/F, Gateway Arcade, Harbour City, Canton Road, Tsim Sha Tsui

listings.name: Choi Lung Restaurant
listings.content: A typical local Chinese restaurant offering dim sum and a Cantonese style dinner. Dim Sum starts from $4.80. It is a nightclub after seven with contemporary music.

listings.name: Dragon Centre Food Court
listings.content: This food court provides a variety of Chinese, Southeast Asian and Western cuisines at attractive prices. Dishes range from $10 up.
listings.address: 8/F, Dragon Centre, 37K Yen Chow Street, Sham Shui Po

listings.name: Fa Yuen Street Complex
listings.content: A complex consisting of a wet market, cooked food centre, sports centre and a public library. It is a place where you can find cheap and genuine Hong Kong style food in Kowloon. There was only one small food stall open on a Sunday afternoon. Maybe better during the week?

listings.name: Mr. Wong's
listings.content: This one is popular with exchange students in Hong Kong, offering all the food you can eat and all the beer you can drink.

listings.name: Swagat
listings.content: On the first floor of Chungking Mansions, this is arguably one of the best Indian restaurants in Hong Kong.

listings.name: Tim Ho Wan
listings.content: It is said to be the cheapest Michelin starred restaurant in the world, serving a variety of dim sum dishes starting at $10. Be prepared to wait one, two or even three hours if you come on a busy day (you get a numbered menu/ticket and can come back later).

listings.name: Jade Palace
listings.content: A tasty and tourist-friendly dim sum spot. Order by selecting from a card (also in English), not from a cart. Try the shrimp and chive dumplings and the tripe in ginger soup. Dim sum served 11AM-3PM daily, dishes $16-40 each.
listings.address: 4/F, Star House, Canton Road, Tsim Sha Tsui

listings.name: Red Ant
listings.content: A modern bistro-like restaurant with a wide selection of light meals and snacks. No alcohol is served but there is a long list of fresh juices and teas.
listings.address: G/F, 27 Ashley Rd, Tsim Sha Tsui

listings.name: Yat Tung Heen
listings.content: Cantonese dishes and dim sum, from traditional favourites to original creations.
listings.address: Eaton Hotel, 380 Nathan Road, Kwun Chung

listings.name: Aberdeen Seafood Restaurant
listings.price: Eat outside on the pavement and watch the world pass you buy in this busy street for pedestrians. Serves goose and other meat dishes in addition to seafood. A cheap place to drink beer

listings.name: Green
listings.content: Contemporary cafe and restaurant located within the modern Hotel Icon. Lunch offers set menus with lobster, pasta and more. Nice desserts and wine list. The interior is beautiful, with one of the world's largest indoor vertical gardens.

listings.name: La Taverna Restaurant
listings.content: Hong Kong's oldest Italian restaurant sits hidden in plain view at the end of busy Ashley Road. Stepping through the door is like stepping back in time to a Hong Kong of the past or at least an Italian version of it circa 1960s. Delicious pastas and meat dishes and risottos to die for. Well worth a visit as much as for a sense of Hong Kong history as the tasty Italian food. A true oasis of tranquility in bustling Kowloon and very reasonably priced.

listings.name: Oi Man Sang
listings.content: This outdoor kitchen may be the last outdoor food stall still cooking over the extreme heat of kerosene, wok hei-style. Expect to stand in line for a bit.
listings.address: Sham Shui Po Building, 1A-1C Shek Kip Mei St

listings.name: Fook Lam Moon
listings.content: The yum cha/dim sum is excellent. The service and decor is also impressive. Expect to pay around $55 per serve for the mid range dishes. The English menu is only a small subset of the Chinese menu so take along someone who can translate to increase your choice of dishes. Another

listings.name: Gaddi's
listings.content: Arguably Hong Kong's leading restaurant that has delighted aficionados of French food and wine for over 80 years. This is the place where you can test your own command of the French language against French-speaking Chinese waiters. You will be disappointed if you are expecting great harbour views.
listings.address: Peninsula Hotel, Salisbury Road, Tsim Sha Tsui

listings.name: Morton's The Steakhouse
listings.content: The Hong Kong location for this famous chain of American steakhouses, Morton's has one best in the city multiple times. With views overlooking the harbour, great service and classic cocktails - combined with thick steaks - makes Morton's a classy and classic experience.

listings.name: Nobu
listings.content: The HK location for this exclusive Japanese restaurant. Nobu has delicate bento box lunches and decadent dinners and desserts. Remarkable service and drinks, and a view overlooking the Harbour that is worth the price. Dress nice and make a reservation if going for dinner.

listings.name: Aqua
listings.content: Nearby at the top of the 1 Peking Road office building is an alternative and less touristy spot with equally impressive views. As well as a bar, they have a Japanese and Italian restaurant for those without a budget.

listings.name: Biergarten
listings.content: This friendly German bar is one of the few places in Kowloon where you can find a good range of quality beers. Excellent German food is served — not just sausages and sauerkraut. Use Exit N2 at East Tsim Sha Tsui MTR station.

listings.name: Felix
listings.content: Atop the Peninsula Hotel on Salisbury Rd, is known for its Philippe Starck interior and the views of the harbour skyline, whilst the men's bathroom has an impressive view up Nathan Road. According to legend, the world's first screwdriver was mixed up here, sampling this simple mix of orange juice and vodka will set you back around $100 a pop.

listings.name: Hutong
listings.content: Hutong is a great place to get a good view of Hong Kong from the top floor of a business building. It's a Michelin starred restaurant with amazing food — try the signature crispy lamb breast with garlic and ginger.

listings.name: Knutsford Terrace
listings.content: Near the Miramar hotel is perhaps best described as the 'Lang Kwai Fong' of Kowloon, and has a large number of bars and restaurants of variable quality that cater for mid-range budgets. A little smaller and less phrenetic than Lan Kwai Fong, but well worth the effort to poke your nose along this narrow street on a Saturday evening.

listings.name: Ashley Road
listings.content: Between Nathan Road and the Ocean Terminal shopping mall, features many Western restaurants and bars.

listings.name: Mody Road/Centennial Garden
listings.content: Close to many good hotels, this area of Tsim Sha Tsui offers a more relaxed environment for a drink. Here you will find bars and restaurants spilling out onto the pavement. Leave East Tsim Sha Tsui station at Exit P1, and head past the Kowloon Shangri-La hotel.

listings.name: Tung Choi Street
listings.content: Between Prince Edward Road and Boundary Street, is one of Kowloon's up-and-coming bar strips. Few tourists or expats venture here, but there are nearly two dozen bars. Some specialize in karaoke while others have open fronts and extensive drink menus. Prince Edward MTR, exit A.

listings.name: Australian guesthouse
listings.content: A clean guesthouse with TV, good Wi-Fi, fridge, hot water, air con and en suite bathroom. The rooms seem to be quite modern and updated although fairly small. Owner is a pretty nice and helpful guy. Room was cleaned and made up every day. Hot water is pretty strong and good! The beds in the twin rooms (sleeps 2) go for about $250.

listings.name: Canadian Hostel
listings.content: Clean guesthouse with TV, fast Wi-Fi, 24 hours cold and hot water. All the rooms are air conditioned and have en suite bathrooms. The rooms are modern. The owner is friendly. The rooms are cleaned and made every day.
listings.address: 7th floor Chungking Mansions, Block E, Flat E6

listings.name: New Fortunate Guesthouse, International Inn
listings.content: One of the nicer guesthouses in the building. Rooms are small but clean and cheerful. A double room with A/C, TV and in-room wireless internet access should cost around $250 per night, perhaps less during low quieter times or for those willing to bargain hard.

listings.name: Travellers Hostel
listings.content: A long-established and with a reasonable reputation.
listings.address: Flat A1 & A2, Block A, 16/F, Chungking Mansions

listings.name: Welcome Guest House
listings.content: Good guest house: doubles go for $180, are fairly roomy and are equipped with AC, fridge, TV, telephone and bathrooms with hot shower and toilet. Singles are $130, are positively tiny and don't have a fridge. Most rooms, apart from those farthest from the reception, have free Wi-Fi. Rooms are clean but mediocre (leaky sinks, some cracked tiles, nothing too serious); sheets are changed and rooms cleaned daily. The biggest problem with this guest house is that some of the air-con units are rather noisy (even when turned off), so if you have trouble sleeping, it's worth bringing your own earplugs. The staff are very friendly and trustworthy. Some travellers report having left their luggage, including rather expensive laptops and Kindles in plain sight in their rooms unattended for several days, and nothing having been taken or tampered with.
listings.address: A Block, 7th floor, Room 5, Chungking Mansions

listings.name: Whole Sunshine Hotel
listings.content: They also own 4th floor but it is being refurbished. Feels like a junior manager's love nest, with circular bed (very firm) and hourly rates. Welcoming, manager has enough English, clean, small room, a/c works but seldom hot water. No room safe.

listings.name: Cosmic Guest House
listings.content: A clean hostel with mostly friendly staff, you can get clean dorms here. or bargain for a good deal on one of the tiny private rooms with air-conditioning and cable TV.

listings.name: Garden Hostel
listings.content: Long-established place, dorm beds with hot water bathrooms. Has a garden to sit in.

listings.name: USA Hostel Hong Kong
listings.content: Located in an old building that is also home to stores and other commercial enterprises, expect a budget hotel which (usually) is clean. Ask to see the room first, or you'll get a really small one. Generally, the next day they will move you out of the good room into one of the smaller ones. Also don't be surprised to see the television and shower not function properly.

listings.name: Dragon Hostel
listings.content: Tiny but clean rooms with aircon and free Internet at reception. Located on the 7th floor and a short walking distance from Mong Kok MTR Station.

listings.name: Hakkas Guest House
listings.content: This well-maintained guesthouse is home to 10 immaculate rooms and is one of the best budget deals at the Yau Ma Tei end of Nathan Rd.
listings.address: Flat l 3/f., 13-15 Jordan Rd, Yau Ma Tei

listings.name: Hop Inn
listings.content: A clean and stylish hostel with friendly staff, one of the best in the Tsim Sha Tsui area. Each room was designed by a different local artist/illustrator (very interesting). They also have another nearby location at 5/F, Lyton Building, 36 Mody Road, Tsim Sha Tsui

listings.name: Lee Garden Guest House
listings.content: Tiny but clean rooms, this hostel is in a great location, near the MTR station and a few blocks from Nathan Road.

listings.name: YHA Mei Ho House Youth Hostel
listings.content: YHA hostel in the Mei Ho House, the last remaining example of a "Mark I" building (historic H-shaped public housing block), formerly part of Shek Kip Mei Estate (the first public housing estate in Hong Kong) and also the base of the rioters during Hong Kong 1956 riots. You can either stay in a modern room or a 1970s themed one. The dormitories are all modern. There is also a museum about early public housing (open Tu-Su 9AM-5PM).

listings.name: Rainbow Lodge HK
listings.content: Clean, convenient, and well-designed hostel on Nathan Road in Tsim Sha Tsui with big lockers, good wifi, air conditioning, and curtains on the bunks. The common area is small but lively, with a refrigerator and microwave. It's in a touristy area, which has both benefits and drawbacks: avoid the restaurants in the immediate area, which seem to be priced out of proportion with their quality.
listings.address: Flat 501, 5/F, Hai Phong Mansion, 101 Nathan Road

listings.name: Chelsea Hotel
listings.content: Quite a bit nicer than the budget places, not a lot more expensive, prime location.
listings.price: $700 for single occupancy in double room
listings.address: Hanoi Road, corner of Mody Rd

listings.name: Eaton Hotel Hong Kong
listings.content: Hotel overlooking Nathan Rd.

listings.name: Harbour Plaza Metropolis
listings.content: Rooms overlooking the harbour. Large outdoor swimming pool.

listings.name: The Salisbury YMCA
listings.content: Hong Kong's main YMCA and a well regarded hotel. All rooms have private bathrooms and some have good views of the harbour. The location, next to the Peninsula Hotel and near the Tsim Sha Tsui MTR station, can't be beaten. Popular with budget-minded families. Reservations well in advance are highly recommended. Other Y services (swimming pool, gym, restaurants, etc.) are available to hotel guests either free or at reasonable rates.

listings.name: Dorsett Mongkok Hotel
listings.content: Provides free use of smart phone with free 4G Internet with IDD facilities to 9 countries, Wi-Fi, mosaic bathroom with massage shower and rain shower head.

listings.name: The Cityview
listings.content: Run by the Chinese YMCA, the former YMCA International House.

listings.name: Park Hotel Hong Kong
listings.content: Refurbished in 2020, and rooms have the amenities one can expect from an upper mid-range hotel in a first-world country. There's a cafe and a bar.
listings.address: 61 – 65 Chatham Road South, Tsim Sha Tsui

listings.name: Regal Oriental Hotel
listings.content: Originally named "Regal Meridien Hong Kong Airport Hotel" and built as the airport hotel for the old Kai Tak Airport, with a footbridge connecting it to the terminal building. The footbridge and terminal building have since been demolished after the airport was closed down in 1998, but the hotel remains standing.

listings.name: Hyatt Regency Hong Kong, Tsim Sha Tsui
listings.content: 381 rooms and suites with views of the harbour and Kowloon skyline, Sky Garden and outdoor pool. Guestroom amenities: work area, marble bath, Wi-Fi. Regency Club Lounge for free continental breakfast, private concierge and secretarial services.

listings.name: Regent Hong Kong
listings.content: On the waterfront, good views of the harbour and the Hong Kong skyline.

listings.name: Kowloon Shangri-La
listings.address: 64 Mody Rd, Tsim Sha Tsui East

listings.name: Langham Hotel Hong Kong
listings.content: An elegant European-style hotel.

listings.name: Cordis Hong Kong
listings.content: Hotel built in 2004. Adjacent to a modern shopping mall.

listings.name: Peninsula Hong Kong
listings.content: Hong Kong's grand old historic hotel has a commanding presence with some of Hong Kong's best bars, restaurants and luxury boutiques (and equally commanding prices starting at around $2,500 per night). Or how about the $50,000 honeymoon suite package including a helicopter tour of the city? The hotel was the venue where British governor Mark Young surrendered to the Japanese and was taken over as a military headquarters during the Japanese occupation in World War II.

listings.name: Regal Kowloon Hotel
listings.content: 600 rooms and suites with Wi-Fi.

listings.name: Hong Kong Disneyland
listings.content: Asia's second Disneyland was opened in September 2005 and features some of the Disney favourites. The park is accessible via the MTR. Change at the Sunny Bay station on the Tung Chung MTR line for the Disneyland Resort Line. It has nine themed areas: Main Street USA, Adventureland, Fantasyland, Tomorrowland, Toy Story Land, Grizzly Gulch, Mystic Point, World of Frozen and Stark Expo. Tickets are $639 for adults, $475 for children, and $100 for Seniors over 65. There are fewer rides than the other Disney theme parks. A few rides have a slightly different take on them, but there is little unique here. Some rides are simply identical to other parks. If you get there at opening time on a weekday, it would be possible to do all the rides and shows by mid-afternoon. English speakers are well catered for, with all attractions narrating in both English and Cantonese. The Jungle River Cruise, however, which depends so much on the English language delivery of the guide doesn't fare well. There is a choice of Cantonese and American cuisine around the park. The Fantasyland Banquet Hall offering the broadest range of food types and kids meals to keep everyone happy. Meals around $55. There are plenty of drinking fountains in the park. Bring a water bottle to fill, or pay a bottle in the park. On weekends and holidays the tickets are $350 for adults and $250 for children. Children under 3 are free. Visit on weekdays to avoid the crowds.

listings.name: Inspiration Lake Recreation Centre
listings.content: Inspiration Lake is the largest artificial lake in Hong Kong, and has a 1500-m jogging trail. It also has an arboretum, and rents paddle boats and surrey bikes. It is in Penny's Bay, a 15-minute walk from Disneyland Resort MTR station, or take the R8 bus.

listings.name: Ngong Ping 360
listings.content: A spectacular 5.7-km cable car journey that takes in an impressive cultural themed village and the Tian Tan Buddha. At the themed village there are a couple of attractions. The Walking with Buddha attraction gives an interesting introduction to Buddha, and has different stages, with headphones giving the narration in a variety of languages. The Monkey's Tail is simply a silent animated movie, with a simple moral. A little trivial overall. Combined tickets can be bought to cover all three attractions. There are about 10 restaurants in the village, serving a variety of food, all a little on the expensive side for what they are. There are some other restaurants in the true village, beyond the themed section. The cable car station is adjacent to the Tung Chung MTR. Note that there are often lengthy queues to go up the mountain, especially on weekends - if the queue extends downstairs, expect a two hour wait. To avoid you can take a bus up the mountain and the cable car back (queues are much shorter, especially if buying the Crystal Cabin). Alternatively, buy a guided tour or the Journey to Enlightenment package, both of which bypass most of the queue for the cheaper tickets.

listings.name: Tian Tan Buddha
listings.content: At over 250 tonnes and 34 in height, this was the largest seated outdoor bronze Buddha statue in the world, until the statue of Dordenna Buddha near Thimphu in Bhutan was finished in 2015. The site also offers unobstructed views over the island. Access to the Buddha is free, although entering the museum inside during busy times requires a meal ticket for the vegetarian restaurant; a snack costs $23 while full meals are $60 (normal) or $100 (deluxe). Less direct alternatives to the cable car are bus #2 from Mui Wo ferry pier or bus #23 from Tung Chung (both $17.20/27 on weekdays/Sundays).

listings.name: Po Lin Monastery
listings.content: The monastery was founded in 1906 by three monks from Jiangsu province. The main temple building houses three bronze statues representing the Buddha of the past, present and future.

listings.name: Tai O
listings.content: A traditional fishing village with houses built on stilts over the sea. Tai O also called "Eastern Venice".

listings.name: Discovery Bay
listings.content: As a residential district, Discovery Bay is not really a tourist destination. However, it boasts a 400-m beach, a golf and marina club for members and guests, meaning that the area attracts day trippers. It also holds festivals, including most notably, dragon boat races at the beach in May/June and a multicultural festival in November.

listings.name: Mui Wo
listings.content: a rural town on the eastern coast of Lantau Island. The main beach in Mui Wo is known as Silver Mine Bay (銀礦灣). There are fast and slow ferry services from Central to Mui Wo. Central - Mui Wo Ferry The fast ferry costs $25 and takes 30 minutes. The slow ferry costs $15, takes 50 minutes and you can go outside. The 3M bus takes you from Tung Chung to Mui Wo. There are a number of temples and old buildings. There is also a waterfall, an old mining cave (sealed off) and numerous hiking trails. Close to the Ferry Pier there are three bicycle rent shops where you rent bikes from $30 to $150. At the beginning of Silver Mine Beach there is also a place to rent bicycles.

listings.name: Lantau Peak
listings.content: At 934 m, the second highest point in Hong Kong and the highest point on Lantau Island. You can also stay overnight at the Ngong Ping hostel, and wake up very early to reach the summit in time for the spectacular sunrise. Although not particularly high by international standards, this is a fairly hard climb and you should make full preparations, especially during summer.

listings.name: The Stoep
listings.content: Beachside restaurant with a good western menu and also specializes in serving South African dishes. Although the food is not the main attraction, the location of this restaurant makes it one of the best places to eat and drink in Hong Kong. Booking a table is advisable at weekends and Public Holidays.

listings.name: High Tide Restaurant
listings.content: Authentic Thai restaurant. Located right on the beach front, you might think you're in Thailand. An ideal place to get refreshments after a lazy day on one of Hong Kong's best beaches.

listings.name: China Beach Club
listings.content: Silvermine Bay (Mui Wo). Head for the beach in the bay and then carry on walking. Serves great food and drinks to the colonial crowd and locals alike. This is a doggie paradise in Hong Kong.

listings.name: The China Bear
listings.content: Mui Wo. Walk off the ferry and turn left and you will see a cafe/bar next to the sea. If you are looking for a "full English" breakfast, or some western beer, then you have found the right place.

listings.name: Deli France
listings.content: Near the MTR.

listings.name: Pizza Hut
listings.content: Near the MTR.

listings.name: Food Republic
listings.content: A large food court that is incredibly busy at lunch and dinner times on weekends with a lot of mainlanders hungry after a hard day of shopping.

listings.name: Olea
listings.content: With floor-to-ceiling glass windows of 7 m looking out to a man-made water and bamboo feature. Olea is a casual fine dining restaurant in the hotel and features an open Mediterranean kitchen, with a pizza oven and an array of various classic tapas and mezze dishes.

listings.name: Essence
listings.content: Located on the lobby level, Essence was designed by a world famous interior designer Yasumichi Morita.It is the main dining venue in the hotel and features international cuisine through buffet and à la carte offerings.

listings.name: 360 Forest Grill & Restaurant Bar
listings.content: Overlooking the cable car, 360 Forest Grill & Restaurant Bar offers alfresco dining in a peaceful, garden setting; only moments away from the hustle of Tung Chung. A wide range of a-la-cart grilled meats and fresh sea foods, three course buffet sets, and standard Asian and European dishes.

listings.name: Hemingway’s by the Bay
listings.content: Beachside dining with 80 indoor seats, 86 outside.

listings.name: China Bear
listings.address: G/F, Mui Wo Ctr, Mui Wo

listings.name: Mcsorley's Ale House
listings.address: Shop G11A, G/F, D Deck, Discovery Bay

listings.name: Starz
listings.content: There are few bar options in Tung Chung, and this is probably the best you are going to find.

listings.name: Novotel Citygate Hong Kong
listings.content: Novotel Citygate Hong Kong is 5 minutes from Hong Kong International Airport with free shuttle service. With direct access to mass transit railway (MTR), it takes 28 minutes to the city centre and Hong Kong Disneyland is 2 stops away.

listings.name: Silver Mine Bay Hotel
listings.content: Swimming pool, sauna, beach side. Breakfast included. 128 room hotel and resort.

listings.name: Ngong Ping SG Davis Hostel at the Po Lin Monastery
listings.content: Reservations made are not always acknowledged upon arrival, but sometimes when you're told they're booked solid you can still get a bunk. You needed to be a member of a Youth Hostel Association in order to get the best rates. Membership is available online.

listings.name: Disney's Hollywood Hotel
listings.content: Themed to represent Art Deco Hollywood

listings.name: Ping Shan Heritage Trail
listings.content: This is a kilometre long trail enabling you to take in the most important buildings in this historical area, including the ancient pagoda of Tsui Sing Lau, the Tang Ancestral Hall and the Kun Ting Study Hall.

listings.name: Maclehose Trail
listings.content: Stage I is ~3 hours, stage II ~6 hours of walking for a total of 10 stages and 100km. Parts are sealed/concrete road, other parts dirt/rock. if you hike late, take a light as public lights are sparse. Altitude is between 0 and 300m (Sai Wan Shan). Camping sites are available.

listings.name: Hong Kong Wetland Park
listings.content: Is a relaxing park set amidst an ecological mitigation area. One can stroll along a network of board walks built over the marshy area and watch birds from a tower. The park also features a large visitors centre/museum. The museum has many interactive exhibits ideal for children, as well as some live animal habitats. To visit, take MTR West Rail to Tin Shui Wai Station, then the #705 light rail to Wetland Park. The park is pushchair and wheelchair friendly.

listings.name: Hong Kong UNESCO Global Geopark
listings.content: Different rock formations and geological features are found here.The park is an area of 150 km2 across parts of the eastern and northeastern New Territories.

listings.name: Tai Mo Shan
listings.content: The highest point in Hong Kong, at about 956 m above sea level or 957 m above the Hong Kong Principal Datum. You hike almost to the summit, but not all the way as the summit houses a weather station and military outpost.

listings.name: Hong Kong Heritage Museum
listings.content: For those with a serious interest in Chinese culture, this might appeal to you as one of Hong Kong's best museums. Modern, informative and attractively presented, this museum houses several permanent exhibitions of life in the New Territories, Cantonese opera, and Chinese art, as well as temporary exhibitions of a high calibre.

listings.name: Hong Kong Railway Museum
listings.content: An open-air museum converted from the old Tai Po Railway Station. It has seven railway coaches and two locomotives.
listings.address: 13 Shung Tak Street, Tai Po Market, Tai Po

listings.name: Jockey Club Museum of Climate Change
listings.address: Yasumoto International Academic Park, 8th Floor, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shatin

listings.name: The Art Museum, The Chinese University of Hong Kong
listings.content: M-W F Sa from 10AM-5PM, Sunday and public holidays from 1:00-5PM, closed Th (except public holidays), New Year, Lunar New Year, Easter, and Christmas holidays. Admission is free.
listings.address: Art Museum, Institute of Chinese Studies, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Sha Tin

listings.name: Tao Heung Museum of Food Culture
listings.content: Museum displays cooking utensils, cutlery, spices from different time periods around the world and the food culture of Hong Kong. Advance online reservation is required. Each session lasts 75 minutes. Guide will narrate in Cantonese for 45 minutes followed by 30 minutes of free tour.
listings.address: 13 Au Pui Wan St, Fo Tan

listings.name: Tsz Shan Monastery Buddhist Art Museum
listings.address: No. 88, Universal Gate Road, Tai Po

listings.name: Sam Tung Uk Museum
listings.content: A Hakka walled-village that was built in 1786.

listings.name: Sha Tau Kok Anti-Japanese War Memorial Hall
listings.content: Opened in September 2022, this is the first comprehensive museum about the Second World War in Hong Kong. The museum is at the former home of the Luo Family, which was the first base of operations for Communist-led guerrilla fighters from the Mainland who came across the border to help resist the Japanese. At the present time, the museum is only accepting group visits and bookings are essential. As the museum is outside the Frontier Closed Area, visitors do not need a permit to visit the museum.
listings.address: 39 Sha Tau Kok Road (Shek Chung Au), Sha Tau Kok

listings.name: Castle Peak Monastery
listings.content: Classed as a Grade I historic building that has been standing for more than 1000 years. These historic monuments have stood through the ages in a tranquil woodland area. The striking and picturesque surroundings create an enjoyable view, as well as a solemn ambiance. Upon entering the monastery, you will notice the words "香海名山" (Fragrant Sea and Prestigious Mountain) engraved on the portico. The Tsing Shan Temple is among the three oldest temples in Hong Kong. Inside the temple, there is a main worship hall. Walking up the stairs leading to the hall, you will see "一切有情、同登覺地" (which means Everything on Earth Has Ties and Reaches Nirvana Together). The peaceful environment of this Buddhist temple offers an abiding sense of harmony.

listings.name: 10,000 Buddhas Monastery
listings.content: This rather garish but enjoyable modern temple dating from the 1950s in fact contains no less than 12,800 Buddhas lining the walls of the main hall.
